items.name: Langit Collective
items.text: A social enterprise that partners with indigenous smallholder farmers in East Malaysia to revive traditional rice growing, buying heirloom rice and crops directly from them, returning at least 35% of retail proceeds to the farmers and reinvesting 30% of profits in training workshops.

items.name: Pandai
items.text: A learning app accredited as a social enterprise by the Ministry of Entrepreneur Development and Cooperatives, with paid Pandai Premium access and company-sponsored devices, data plans and scholarships that bring it to students who cannot afford it, from SPM candidates to PPR communities in three states.

items.name: MYReaders
items.text: A community-driven reading programme that runs English literacy interventions, small reading groups, teacher training and Orang Asli parent mentors, and has reached over 36,000 students, 2,000 parents and 1,100 teachers in 144 schools and 67 communities.

items.name: EPIC Homes
items.text: An award-winning social enterprise that builds homes with the indigenous Orang Asli of Peninsular Malaysia through team-building programmes for companies, and has provided safe homes for over 350 families, mobilising more than 9,000 people and 200 organisations since 2010.

items.name: PichaEats
items.text: A social enterprise, founded in 2016, that turns the home cooking of refugee families into catering income; it has partnered with over 40 refugee chefs, served more than 1,000 clients and channelled over MYR 7 million back to the community.

items.name: Batik Boutique
items.text: A B Corp-certified social enterprise that sells handcrafted batik apparel and works with low-income women, refugees and artisans from marginalised communities, employing around 400 artisans who made over 20,000 pieces in 2025 for its four stores in the Klang Valley.

items.name: The Asli Co.
items.text: A social enterprise whose pots, soaps, tote bags and other goods are made at home by indigenous Orang Asli mothers, more than 60 from eight villages, who earn about RM600 a month on average.

dispatches.label: 16 Nov 2026
dispatches.author: steward
dispatches.title: Malaysia approves a RM19.05 billion SDG sukuk programme for the ECRL
dispatches.summary: The Government of Malaysia has approved Malaysia Rail Link’s fifth sukuk programme, worth RM19.05 billion, issued as SDG sukuk to help finance the RM52.43 billion East Coast Rail Link, weeks before commercial operations are due to begin.
body: On 16 November 2026 the Government of Malaysia approved Malaysia Rail Link’s fifth sukuk programme, worth RM19.05 billion. Finance Minister II Datuk Seri Amir Hamzah Azizan announced it at a Tokenised Sukuk Initiative ceremony held with CIMB Group at the ECRL Gombak Integrated Terminal Station, as reported by Bernama and carried by the Ministry of Finance.

The sukuk will be issued as United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) sukuk, following Malaysia Rail Link’s third and fourth SDG sukuk programmes. The report does not state the tenor, the profit rate or the terms of any guarantee; those will be known when the programme is issued.

The programme helps finance the East Coast Rail Link, a RM52.43 billion project undertaken by the Malaysian government. A RM37.40 billion term loan from the Export-Import Bank of China carries a 3.25 per cent interest rate; local banking institutions finance the remainder through sukuk. The Kota Bharu to Gombak alignment was 98.5 per cent complete as of October 2026, and commercial operations are targeted to begin on 12 December 2026.
Of the seven standards, the line moves livelihood first: it links the east coast states to the Klang Valley, widening access to jobs and markets for the communities along its route.

The structure could work for another nation. Kenya, which financed its own standard gauge railway largely with bilateral loans, could refinance or extend such a line by pairing its domestic Islamic and green bond markets with a long-dated SDG-labelled issue placed with local banks.
